title: Make mercy your mosque
hookLine: make mercy your mosque, faith your prayer mat, honest earning your Qur'an (Majh ki Var M1, ang 140)

lines: IN THE LANGUAGE OF THEIR PRACTICE.
cards: Guru Nanak spent his life among both Muslims and Hindus. Tradition remembers his companion on the road, Bhai Mardana, as a Muslim musician who played the rabab beside him.

In the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak often speaks to people in the language of their own practice. To Hindus he talks about the sacred thread, the pilgrimage, the lamp. To Muslims, the mosque, the prayer mat, the fast.
And in one salok in Majh ki Var, he builds a whole mosque without a single brick.

teach.h: MERCY THE MOSQUE, FAITH THE MAT.
teach.b: It goes, in effect: make mercy your mosque, faith your prayer mat, and what is honest and rightfully earned your Qur'an. Make modesty and good conduct your observances and your fast; so become a Muslim.
Make good deeds your Kaaba, truth your guide, and good works your creed and your prayer. Let your rosary be whatever pleases Him. Then, Nanak, He will keep your honor.
The word for mercy is mihar: kindness, compassion.

teach.h: NOT GIVING IT UP: FILLING IT.
teach.b: It would be easy to hear this wrongly, as Guru Nanak telling Muslims to give up their mosques. That's not what the text says. He doesn't ask anyone to stop praying, fasting or going to the mosque.

He asks what all of it is for, and answers: mercy, faith, honest living, truth, good deeds. It's the same move he makes toward Hindus in Asa di Var, describing a sacred thread spun from compassion and contentment.
In both, he speaks from inside the listener's own words.

teach.h: THE QUESTION TURNS BACK ON SIKHS.
teach.b: For Sikhs, the question turns right back on themselves. What makes a gurdwara a gurdwara? What is the turban for, the Ardas, the langar?
Read that way, the salok's question fits every house of worship, a gurdwara included.
A person can kneel on the finest prayer mat in the world, or bow before the Guru Granth Sahib, and still need to ask whether mercy came in with them.

how: Sikhs sing and recite Majh ki Var in the gurdwara, and often cite this salok of Guru Nanak as teaching that every outward practice is fulfilled through mercy, faith and honest living.

o: faith, a steady trust in God
a prayer mat for daily prayer

games.q: mercy your mosque — tap the pairs.

s: Guru Nanak tells Muslims to stop going to the mosque
he asks what the practices are for, and answers: mercy, faith, honest living.
Guru Nanak speaks to Hindus in the same way
in Asa di Var, a sacred thread spun from compassion and contentment.
Bhai Mardana, Guru Nanak's companion, was a Muslim musician
tradition says he traveled with Guru Nanak and played as the Guru sang.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak, speaking to a Muslim friend about prayer. what do you say?
o: make mercy your mosque and faith your prayer mat.
pray the way I do instead.
games.why: he speaks inside his friend's own words, asking what each practice is for, never using it as a foil.

practice: Picture walking into the place where you pray, rest or find quiet, a mosque, a gurdwara, a church, a bench by a lake, your own bedroom, and ask Guru Nanak's question: did mercy come in with me?
Then think of one small, real merciful act: a patient answer, a meal shared, a debt forgiven, a kind word to someone struggling. If you pray, you can say Waheguru and hold that act before the One.

wordCard.voice: Mihar, mercy, kindness: Guru Nanak, speaking in Islam's own words, makes it the mosque, faith the prayer mat, honest living the Qur'an.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: mercy, kindness; mihar maseet, mercy the mosque.

carryVoice: Your line: mercy is the mosque. What is all of it for? That's day six hundred fifty-four.

sources.ref: Majh ki Var, salok M1, Ang 140–141 (mihar maseet sidak musallaa)
Asa di Var, salok M1, Ang 471 (daiaa kapaah santokh soot)
